extracted.intended_audience: researchers reporting observational epidemiology studies (authors of cohort, case-control, cross-sectional papers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for authors on how to report methods and results of observational studies (cohort, case-control, cross-sectional) to allow readers to judge validity and applicability. Focuses on participant selection, measurement, bias, sample size, variable handling, and statistical methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility criteria and selection description
rubrics_metrics.description: Report all eligibility criteria and describe the group from which the study population was selected and the method of recruitment (e.g., referral or self-selection through advertisements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigators usually restrict a study population by defining clinical, demographic and other characteristics of eligible participants. Typical eligibility criteria relate to age, gender, diagnosis and comorbid conditions. Eligibility criteria may be presented as inclusion and exclusion criteria, although this distinction is not always necessary or useful. Authors should report all eligibility criteria because inadequate reporting impedes readers' understanding of applicability (examples show many reports omit eligibility criteria).

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow-up procedures and completeness of ascertainment
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe the methods used for following participants, whether those methods were the same for all participants, and the completeness of ascertainment of variables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Knowing details about follow-up procedures (e.g., intervals between tests) informs judgments about validity and potential missed events. Authors should state whether procedures minimized non-response and loss to follow-up and whether they were similar for all participants. Differences in follow-up between groups can introduce substantial bias (e.g., unequal ascertainment of events). See also item 14 (presumably outcomes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of cases and controls (case-control studies)
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe how cases and controls were chosen and justify the method of sampling controls so that controls reflect the population from which cases arose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Various methods (population roster sampling, random digit dialing, neighbourhood or friend controls, hospital controls) have advantages and disadvantages. Neighbourhood/friend controls may produce intrinsic matching on exposure; controls with other diseases may better reflect hospital catchment populations but can be problematic if the exposure affects the control disease risk. Often a mixture of defensible control diseases is used. The choice of cases and controls has major implications for validity and must be described.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting of matching (matched cohort and case-control studies)
rubrics_metrics.description: For matched studies give matching criteria and the number of exposed/unexposed (cohort) or the number of controls per case (case-control).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide precise matching criteria and counts. Examples: propensity-based matching protocol (describe steps taken) and statement of attempts to select N controls per case with explanation when some cases lacked the target number. Matching makes groups comparable at baseline and may increase precision, but may require accounting for matching in analysis. The rationale and details of matching methods should be described.

rubrics_metrics.name: Considerations and pitfalls of matching
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain the rationale for choosing matching variables and the method, and be aware of disadvantages such as overmatching and loss of ability to study matching factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Matching is common in case-control studies but has intricacies. Types include frequency (group) matching and individual matching. Poor reporting (e.g., unclear meaning of 'within five years') can mask residual confounding. Overmatching can reduce efficiency and introduce bias if matching variable is closely associated with exposure or lies on the causal pathway. Matching may mandate matched/stratified analysis; consider whether measuring and adjusting for a factor might be preferable to matching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of variables (outcomes, exposures, confounders, effect modifiers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Clearly define all outcomes, exposures, predictors, potential confounders, and effect modifiers; give diagnostic criteria where applicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should define all variables considered for and included in analysis, including diagnostic criteria for disease outcomes (cases in case-control, disease events in cohort, prevalent disease in cross-sectional). Use precise terminology (determinant/predictor, endpoint, dependent/independent) but distinguish exposures from confounders. If many variables measured in exploratory phases, provide detailed lists in appendices or separate publications. Declare all 'candidate variables' considered for statistical analysis rather than selectively reporting final-model variables (see item 16a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Data sources and measurement methods
rubrics_metrics.description: For each variable of interest give sources of data and details of methods of assessment (measurement); describe comparability of assessment methods across groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measurement affects reliability and validity; report findings of validity/reliability studies including reference standards and estimated validity/reliability rather than only citing validation studies. Describe batch processing (e.g., matched samples analyzed together) and whether lab personnel were blinded to case/control status. State if groups differed in data collection methods (which can cause bias) and any quality-control programs used to prevent measurement 'drift'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bias: reporting efforts to address potential sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe any efforts to address potential sources of bias, assess the likelihood of relevant biases, and discuss direction and magnitude (estimate if possible).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Biased studies systematically deviate from truth; authors should consider potential sources of bias during design and report measures taken to reduce bias at reporting stage. Examples include selecting appropriate control groups to reduce information bias and collecting additional data to adjust for detection bias. Quality-control programmes for data collection should be described. Authors should not ignore important biases—surveys show many studies fail to address bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions and examples of information and selection bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand and report whether observed issues arise from information bias or selection bias and how they were addressed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Information bias: systematic differences in completeness/accuracy of data (detection bias, recall bias, interviewer bias); mitigation includes blinding and randomising order of interviewing. Selection bias: when inclusion probabilities are associated with exposure (e.g., diagnostic or registry submission biases) or response bias (differences between responders and non-responders). Selection bias affects internal validity while participant selection for generalisability affects external validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study size: rationale and sample size determination
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain how the study size was arrived at; give a priori sample size calculations if done or indicate considerations that determined study size.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A study should be large enough to produce sufficiently narrow confidence intervals for the research question. Formal a priori calculations may be useful when planning new studies, but are uncertain due to assumptions. If analysis uses pre-existing data, explain whether statistical precision is adequate. Report if a study was stopped early for statistical significance. Avoid post hoc justifications or retrospective power calculations; present confidence intervals to show precision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grouping of continuous data
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain reasons for grouping continuous data and the choice of cut-points, acknowledging consequences of grouping.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grouping can simplify presentation or avoid implausible precision, but loses information and reduces statistical power, particularly with dichotomization, and may produce residual confounding. Increasing categories can reduce power loss. Cut-points may be based on clinical relevance, practicality, or quantiles; in case-control studies, deriving distribution from controls is preferred. Inform readers if cut-points were selected post hoc (which may exaggerate associations). When analysing grouped variables, consider underlying continuous nature and examine trends; publish both categorical and continuous estimates to facilitate meta-analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling of quantitative variables in analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain how quantitative variables were handled, including chosen groupings and rationale; report category counts and consider modelling choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should report number of categories, cut-points, and category means/medians, and give counts (cases, controls, persons at risk, person-time) per category. Consider modelling exposures as continuous to retain information, but check for non-linearity and investigate alternatives (log transform, quadratic terms, spline functions). Report alternative models explored and consider presenting both continuous and grouped analyses for key exposures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical methods and confounding control
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe all statistical methods used, including methods to control for confounding, variable selection procedures, and other analytic choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is no single correct analysis; authors should pre-specify analyses for primary objectives and clarify which analyses were data-driven. Describe procedures for variable selection rather than only final-model results; explain model comparisons and which covariates contribute to confounding. Describe methods such as stratification, multivariable regression (specify type appropriate to design, e.g., Cox for cohorts, logistic for case-control), imputation, transformations, attributable risk calculations, and any non-standard approaches (with references). Report statistical software. Provide enough detail to enable a knowledgeable reader with the original data to verify results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subgroup and interaction analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe methods used to examine subgroups and interactions and clarify whether analyses were pre-specified or exploratory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subgroup analyses are debated but commonly performed; authors should describe methods (e.g., testing for biological interaction using composite variables, calculation of measures such as RERI, and CI methods). Clarify the rationale and report how interactions were tested and interpreted.
